analysis.one_liner: Creates an FTC cybersecurity office to police credit bureaus' data security and fine them for breaches.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in the final month of the 118th Congress and referred to the Banking Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or any Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new Office of Cybersecurity inside the Federal Trade Commission with authority to write and enforce data-security rules for the big consumer reporting agencies — the companies like Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion that collect and sell Americans' credit files, Social Security numbers, and other sensitive personal data [S2]. Agencies would have to report breaches to the FTC within 10 days and notify affected consumers, and the FTC could sue for mandatory penalties of $100 per consumer plus $50 per additional item of exposed data, capped at 50% of the bureau's gross revenue (75% if the bureau failed to follow the security rules or report on time) [S2]. Half of penalty money would fund cybersecurity enforcement and half would go to consumers harmed in the breach [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose financial lives are cataloged by credit bureaus. Anyone whose name, Social Security number, or account number is exposed in a breach would be notified and entitled to a share of the penalty, and stronger required security measures would reduce the odds of a repeat of the 2017 Equifax breach, which exposed the personal data of roughly 147 million Americans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data credit bureaus hold

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered consumer reporting agencies to meet detailed security standards — encryption of data at rest and in transit, network monitoring, patch management, vulnerability testing, and data minimization — and lets the FTC sue to force compliance [S2].
Mandates that a bureau tell the FTC within 10 days of a breach and notify every affected consumer and the public, with only limited law-enforcement delays [S2].

Imposes automatic civil penalties — $100 per consumer whose name plus one other item of data was exposed, plus $50 per additional item, doubled up to 75% of gross revenue if the bureau skipped the security rules or missed the reporting deadline — with half the money paid to affected consumers [S2].
Preserves consumers' right to sue under state or other federal law, on top of the FTC penalty [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies, chiefly Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, which would bear the cost of building security systems to the required standards and of penalties after any breach. Congress would appropriate up to $100 million to set up and run the new office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Equifax, Experian, TransUnion, and similar bureaus

drawbacks.text: The penalty formula is mechanical: a breach exposing even one piece of data triggers $100 per affected consumer, so a large breach could produce penalties in the billions and approach the 50%-of-revenue cap, costs a bureau could pass along through the price of credit services.

A covered breach is defined as exposure of even a single piece of personally identifying information, which the FTC itself could expand further, leaving bureaus exposed to litigation over trivial incidents.

The bill allows notification to consumers to be delayed if federal law enforcement or intelligence agencies say it would impede an investigation, and gives those agencies immunity for delaying — a carve-out that could keep victims in the dark [S2].

It layers a new FTC office on top of existing oversight of the bureaus by the FTC and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, raising the familiar objection that duplicative regulation raises costs without clearly improving security.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: credit bureaus profit by aggregating extremely sensitive data on nearly every American, and today a security failure costs them little while costing breach victims years of identity-theft risk. Per-breach penalties tied to the number of people harmed would give the bureaus a direct financial reason to secure that data. The honest counterweights are the rigid penalty formula (which punishes small and trivial breaches as harshly as huge ones), the law-enforcement delay carve-out, and the fact that no amount of paperwork guarantees a breach never happens. On balance the bill's benefits to consumers plausibly outweigh its costs, though its design is blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 5, 2024, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where it stayed until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4].

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill with Senators Mark Warner and Jeanne Shaheen as cosponsors, both Democrats [S2][S3].

The Senate's only actions were to read the bill twice and refer it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on the day of introduction; the committee took no action before the Congress ended [S4].
Introduced in the final month of a Congress, with two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, the bill never reached a committee hearing or a floor vote [S1][S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies. Because the bill died without a vote, Equifax, Experian, TransUnion, and other bureaus never faced mandatory security standards, breach-reporting deadlines, or automatic per-consumer penalties, and the status quo of modest fines and delayed disclosures remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill reached no vote, so no roll-call party split exists, but its support was entirely on one side of the aisle [S3].

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion and similar bureaus)
industries.note: These firms profit by holding Social Security numbers, account numbers, and credit files on virtually every American, and under current law a breach costs them comparatively little while victims bear identity-theft risk for years. The bill would require security upgrades, 10-day breach reporting, and automatic penalties of up to 50-75% of gross revenue paid partly to victims [S2].
The bill's mandated inventories, encryption, penetration testing, and annual FTC examinations would create demand for the security engineering and audit work needed to meet the standards [S2].

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and identity-theft protection providers
industries.note: Stronger security and victim compensation would reduce demand for paid credit-freeze and monitoring services, though breach-notification requirements could also drive consumers to purchase protection after any incident.
